once.e: From Middle English ones, from Old English ānes, a remodelling (after ān (“one”)) of ǣnes, itself an extension of ǣne (“once”) with the genitive suffix -es. Equivalent to one + -s.

one.e: From Middle English oon, on, oan, an, from Old English ān (“one”), from Proto-West Germanic *ain, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“single, one”). North Frisian ån (“one”); Saterland Frisian aan (“one”); West Frisian ien (“one”); Dutch een, één (“one”); German Low German een; German ein, eins (“one”); Danish en (“one”).
one.g: The number represented by the Arabic numeral 1; the numerical value equal to that cardinal number.

one.e: Analogous to several senses of Hokkien 個／个 (ê) and Mandarin 的 (de, declarative particle, nominalizer, etc.). This semantic loan might have stemmed from the apparent similarity between one as a prop-word and 的 (de) or 個 /个 (ê) as a nominalizer (e.g. 青色的 (“the green one”)).
one.g: Used at the end of a sentence to highlight the characteristics of someone or something.

one's.e: From Middle English ones, equivalent to one + -'s.
Contraction of one + is, equivalent to one + 's.

oneself.e: A contracted form of one's self (Mid-16th century). Equivalent to one + -self.

ongoing.e: From on + going, related to the phrasal verb go on.

oni.g: A Japanese evil spirit or demon.

onion.e: From Middle English onyoun, oynoun, from Old French oignon, from Latin ūniōnem, accusative of ūniō (“onion”), which had also been borrowed into Old English as yne, ynnelēac (“onion”) (> Middle English hynne-leac, henne-leac). The word filter was implemented in relation to the "alpha onion eater" meme, which is depicted as the direct opposite of the soy boy.
onion.g: A monocotyledonous plant (Allium cepa), allied to garlic, used as vegetable and spice.

only.e: From Middle English oonly, only, from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz. By surface analysis, on(e) + -ly. Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one.

onslaught.e: From on- + slaught. Formed after Middle Dutch aenslag, aenslach, equivalent to aen + slag, although slaught corresponds to Middle Dutch slacht; slag is cognate with the English weaving term sley.

onto.g: Arriving upon or on top of (speaking of a physical or metaphorical movement).

onycha.g: the operculum of kinds of strombus or muricid, smoked as an ingredient in the Mosaic incense and pre-modern medicine

onyx.e: From Middle English onix (c. 1300), earlier oniche (c. 1250), from Old French oniche or onix, from Latin onyx, from Ancient Greek ὄνυξ (ónux, “onyx”).
onyx.g: A banded variety of chalcedony, a cryptocrystalline form of quartz.
